articles.title: Big Picture: This week's images from the South of England
articles.summary: The best images sent to us from Berkshire, Dorset, Hampshire, the Isle of Wight and Oxfordshire.
articles.body:
Our Weather Watchers have been out and about taking some beautiful autumnal photos from across the south of England.

Join us as we take a few moments to relax and enjoy the beauty of Oxfordshire, Berkshire, Dorset, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight through the pictures that have been sent to us over the past seven days.

Upload your images via BBC Weather Watchers or email us at southweather@bbc.co.uk . For inspiration, view some top tips from three of England's Big Picture photographers.

When emailing pictures, please make sure you include the following information:

The full name of the person who took the pictures (as this person owns the copyright)

Confirmation that the copyright holder gives permission for the BBC to use their pictures across all its outputs

The location, date and time the pictures were taken

Your telephone number so we can get back to you if we have any further questions

Any other details about the pictures that may be useful for us to know

Please note that while we welcome all your pictures, we are more likely to use those which have been taken in the past week.

Pictures can be found on Instagram , on the hashtags #bbcsouthnews and #BigPicture

If you submit a picture, you do so in accordance with the BBC's Terms and Conditions and the BBC's privacy policy .

In contributing to the South's Big Picture you agree to grant us a royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to publish and otherwise use the material in any way that we want, and in any media worldwide.

It's important to note, however, that you still own the copyright to everything you contribute and that if your image is accepted, we will publish your name alongside.

The BBC cannot guarantee that all pictures will be used and we reserve the right to edit your comments.

At no time should you endanger yourself or others, take any unnecessary risks or infringe any laws while collecting any kind of media.

articles.title: Fiscalização interdita duas academias por irregularidades em Campos | G1
articles.standfirst: Fiscalização da Sedcon, Procon-RJ e Cref1 encontrou irregularidades como ausência de responsável técnico, saída de emergência, alvará de funcionamento e problemas de acessibilidade.
articles.summary: Fiscalização da Sedcon, Procon-RJ e Cref1 encontrou irregularidades como ausência de responsável técnico, saída de emergência e alvará de funcionamento.
articles.body:
Em uma das unidades, também foi constatada a falta de registro do CNPJ junto ao Cref1. — Foto: FTS; Procon RJ

Duas academias foram interditadas em Campos dos Goytacazes , no Norte Fluminense, durante uma fiscalização realizada nesta quarta-feira (4).

A ação foi conduzida pela Secretaria de Estado de Defesa do Consumidor (Sedcon), pelo Procon-RJ e pelo Conselho Regional de Educação Física da 1ª Região (Cref1).

Entre as irregularidades encontradas estavam a ausência de responsável técnico, de saída de emergência e de alvará de funcionamento, além de problemas de acessibilidade. Em uma das unidades, também foi constatada a falta de registro do CNPJ junto ao Cref1.

A fiscalização identificou ainda que um profissional que atuava em um dos estabelecimentos estava com a habilitação em Suporte Básico de Vida vencida.

Outras irregularidades incluíam a ausência do Certificado de Aprovação do Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Estado do Rio de Janeiro. Nos banheiros, as equipes encontraram falta de barras de apoio e espaço insuficiente para manobras de cadeiras de rodas.

Em uma das academias, a catraca de entrada também não tinha dimensões adequadas para a passagem de cadeirantes.

Segundo a Sedcon, as interdições foram motivadas pelos riscos à saúde e à segurança dos frequentadores.

Os dois estabelecimentos permanecerão fechados até que as irregularidades relacionadas à ausência de responsável técnico e de saída de emergência sejam corrigidas e comprovadas junto ao Procon-RJ.

articles.title: Poste no meio da rua em São José dos Campos gera riscos | G1
articles.standfirst: Moradores do Parque Interlagos dizem que a estrutura está no local há cinco anos, apresenta sinais de desgaste e oferece riscos a quem passa pela via.
articles.summary: Poste no meio da rua em São José dos Campos preocupa moradores do Parque Interlagos devido ao desgaste da estrutura e ao risco de acidentes na Rua dos Pinheirinhos.
articles.body:
Moradores do Parque Interlagos, na zona sul de São José dos Campos (SP), reclamam de um poste e de uma caixa de energia instalados no meio da Rua dos Pinheirinhos. Um vídeo enviado ao g1 mostra a estrutura, que, segundo a vizinhança, está no local há cerca de cinco anos.

O poste é de ferro e apresenta sinais de desgaste. A caixa de energia, segundo a comunidade, também não recebe manutenção. Os moradores afirmam ainda que os fios ficam baixos e expostos, o que aumenta o risco para quem circula pela rua.

A EDP informou que, quando há alterações viárias, como mudanças em calçadas ou ruas, a concessionária deve ser acionada pelo órgão municipal responsável para realizar a remoção ou o remanejamento de postes.

Esse é o caso da Rua dos Pinheirinhos, no bairro Interlagos, em São José dos Campos, onde um poste está instalado no meio da via. A concessionária informou que já está em contato com a Prefeitura.

A Prefeitura, por sua vez, informou que fará uma vistoria no local para avaliar quais medidas podem ser adotadas. Sobre o poste, a administração municipal afirmou que vai notificar a EDP.

Em relação à caixa de energia instalada no meio da rua, a Prefeitura informou que o equipamento não pertence ao patrimônio público e, por isso, não é de sua responsabilidade.

articles.title: IBGE oferece 1.527 vagas temporárias para recenseador no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Selecionados irão atuar no 12º Censo Agropecuário, Florestal e Aquícola. Veja como se candidatar.
articles.summary: Selecionados irão atuar no 12º Censo Agropecuário, Florestal e Aquícola.
articles.body:
O Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) oferta 1.527 vagas temporárias de recenseador no Ceará, para atuação no 12º Censo Agropecuário, Florestal e Aquícola.

Os interessados podem se inscrever até as 23h59 do dia 25 de novembro de 2026 , no site da Fundação Cesgranrio , com o pagamento da taxa de R$ 70 .

Segundo o IBGE, os recenseadores receberão salário mensal de R$ 1.741 , além de pagamento por produtividade. Também estão previstos benefícios como auxílio-alimentação de R$ 1.192 , auxílio pré-escolar, 13º salário proporcional, férias proporcionais acrescidas de um terço constitucional e auxílio para custeio dos deslocamentos.

IBGE oferece 1.527 vagas temporárias para recenseador no Ceará. — Foto: Reprodução

As oportunidades exigem ensino fundamental completo e estão distribuídas por municípios de todo o estado. O processo seletivo contará com prova objetiva marcada para 31 de janeiro de 2027 .

Os profissionais selecionados deverão visitar estabelecimentos agropecuários, entrevistar produtores rurais, atualizar mapas e endereços das áreas de trabalho, registrar informações nos dispositivos eletrônicos de coleta e participar de treinamentos e atividades de acompanhamento da operação censitária.

O 12º Censo Agropecuário, Florestal e Aquícola terá coleta nacional prevista para 2027 e produzirá informações para o conhecimento da realidade do campo brasileiro, subsidiando políticas públicas, pesquisas e decisões voltadas ao desenvolvimento do setor agropecuário.

articles.title: Em mensagem de renúncia, Peña pede desculpas e diz que 'nenhuma pessoa está acima do Paraguai'; leia a íntegra | G1
articles.standfirst: Mais cedo, o Congresso do país havia tomado os primeiros passos para votar um impeachment contra Santiago Peña e seu vice. A crise começou após o banco digital Ueno fechar as portas e deixar milhares de clientes sem acesso ao próprio dinheiro. Peña foi acionista do banco.
articles.summary: Mais cedo, o Congresso do país havia tomado os primeiros passos para votar um impeachment contra Santiago Peña e seu vice. A crise começou após o banco digital Ueno fechar as portas e deixar milhares de clientes sem acesso ao próprio dinheiro. Peña foi acionista do banco.
articles.body:
Santiago Penã anuncia renúncia — Foto: Reprodução/X

O presidente do Paraguai , Santiago Peña, renunciou ao cargo nesta quinta-feira (5), em meio a uma crise política. Em comunicado divulgado em suas redes socias, Penã pediu desculpas ao povo e afirmou que "nenhum cargo pode estar acima do bem-estar do Paraguai".

Mais cedo, o Congresso do país havia tomado os primeiros passos para votar um impeachment contra Peña e seu vice.

➡️ A crise começou após o banco digital Ueno fechar as portas e deixar milhares de clientes sem acesso ao próprio dinheiro. Peña foi acionista do grupo que controla a instituição, e a oposição acusa o Banco Central paraguaio de encobrir irregularidades.

Leia abaixo a íntegra do comunicado lido por Penã:

"Queridos compatriotas, hoje me dirijo a vocês em um dos momentos mais difíceis da minha vida, com o coração voltado para o Paraguai e com a convicção de que a nossa República deve estar sempre acima de qualquer pessoa ou circunstância.

A história se encarregará de julgar e colocar na sua devida dimensão os acontecimentos que hoje nos toca viver. Tomei a decisão de apresentar minha renúncia à Presidência da República. Faço isso pensando na estabilidade do nosso país, na paz social e na necessidade de preservar as nossas instituições democráticas.

Faço-o com absoluto respeito à nossa Constituição Nacional e aos mecanismos institucionais e democráticos que estabelecemos para nós mesmos como nação. Estou convencido de que nenhum cargo pode estar acima do bem-estar do Paraguai.

Também quero pedir desculpas ao povo, caso eu tenha falhado em algum momento; nunca foi minha intenção defraudar a confiança que depositaram em mim. Assumi esta responsabilidade todos os dias com a vontade de trabalhar pelo Paraguai, mas hoje a minha prioridade é uma só: a tranquilidade dos paraguaios que confiaram suas economias ao nosso sistema financeiro. Por trás de cada depósito, há anos de esforço, sacrifício e projetos familiares.

Meu maior desejo é que se garanta a devolução desses recursos, que o Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos cumpra a sua finalidade e que sejam protegidos os fundos públicos e os recursos que pertencem a todos os paraguaios.

Queridos compatriotas, somos um país que atravessou momentos muito difíceis e que sempre soube se reerguer. Confio profundamente na força do nosso povo e na capacidade das nossas instituições para superar esta situação.

Hoje, devemos demonstrar, mais uma vez, que a democracia é respeitada, que as instituições são preservadas e que o Paraguai está acima das nossas diferenças. Nenhum cargo é mais importante do que a estabilidade da República; nenhuma pessoa está acima do Paraguai.

Agradeço pela confiança, por cada momento vivido e por terem me dado a honra de servir a esta grande nação. Que Deus abençoe cada família paraguaia e que Deus abençoe o Paraguai."

articles.title: VÍDEO: Turistas flagram onças-pintadas atravessando Rio de RO  | G1
articles.standfirst: Cena foi registrada por um casal que navegava pelo rio quando encontraram os animais. Nas imagens é possível observar três onças, sendo uma delas mais a frete e as outras duas nadando lado a lado
articles.summary: Onças-pintadas nadando foram registradas por um casal no Rio Mequéns, em Rondônia, durante um passeio de barco na fronteira com a Bolívia; assista ao flagrante.
articles.body:
Três onças-pintadas foram flagradas atravessando o Rio Mequéns, na região do distrito de Rolim de Moura do Guaporé, em Alta Floresta d'Oeste (RO), na fronteira com a Bolívia. A cena foi registrada por um casal que navegava pelo rio na segunda-feira (2).

O vídeo foi gravado por Sindinara Gilioli e Gleyck Belmino. Nas imagens, é possível ver três onças nadando pelo rio. Uma delas segue à frente, enquanto as outras duas vêm logo atrás, lado a lado. Em seguida, os animais alcançam a margem e entram na mata.

Ao g1 , Sindinara contou que ela e o marido voltavam de uma pousada localizada no lado boliviano, acompanhados do piloto conhecido como Pirata, quando avistaram os animais. O encontro aconteceu cerca de dez minutos antes de chegarem ao distrito de Rolim de Moura do Guaporé.

"A princípio, imaginamos que fossem capivaras. Mas, à medida que nos aproximávamos, percebemos que havia algo diferente. Então veio a surpresa: três lindas onças atravessando o rio, em seu habitat natural, nadando tranquilamente pelas águas do Rio Mequéns", relatou.

O casal havia viajado para aproveitar o feriado e pescar na região. Segundo Sindinara, a pescaria já estava sendo especial, mas o encontro com as onças tornou a experiência ainda mais marcante.

"Ver uma onça-pintada já é algo extraordinário, mas encontrar três juntas e conseguir registrar esse momento é um privilégio. São situações que mostram a riqueza da nossa região e reforçam a importância de preservar a natureza. Foi uma mistura de surpresa, admiração e muita emoção. Ficamos extremamente felizes e agradecidos por viver uma experiência tão especial", disse.

Ela afirma que a cena ficará para sempre na memória do casal.

articles.title: Morre passageiro ferido após bandeira do PI cair e atingir ônibus  | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu no dia 29 de outubro e deixou um homem e uma mulher gravemente feridos.
articles.summary: Morre o passageiro Edilson Lima, que estava internado após uma estrutura de bandeira atingir um ônibus na Ponte Juscelino Kubitschek, em Teresina, no dia 29 de outubro.
articles.body:
Edilson Lima , de 49 anos, passageiro que ficou ferido após a estrutura de uma bandeira do Piauí atingir um ônibus na ponte Juscelino Kubitschek, na Avenida Frei Serafim , em Teresina , morreu nesta quarta-feira (5). O acidente aconteceu na última quinta-feira, no dia 29 de outubro, e deixou duas pessoas em estado grave.

O impacto resultou em um traumatismo craniano grave na vítima. Segundo o técnico de enfermagem José Orlando, partes da estrutura teriam atingido o ônibus e provocado ferimentos em Edilson e uma mulher. A dinâmica que provocou a queda da placa ainda é apurada pelos órgãos responsáveis.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Governo do Piauí, e o órgão afirmou que ainda aguarda a apuração das circunstâncias do acidente.

A vítima ficou internada por seis dias no HUT após o acidente. Não foram divulgadas informações sobre o estado de saúde da mulher que também foi hospitalizada após o acidente.

No momento do acidente, o ônibus seguia no sentido Centro-Leste e levava vários passageiros. Segundo José Orlando, o motorista do veículo tentou evitar a colisão, mas não conseguiu desviar a tempo.

A família da vítima afirma que o corpo de Edilson será sepultado em Castelo do Piauí, onde a maioria dos parentes e amigos vivem.

articles.title: Ataque de piratas no Amazonas: moradores fogem para mata em Coari | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens mostram uma mulher desesperada com os filhos em meio à mata. Ela relata que passou a noite no local após os criminosos invadirem sua casa e levarem os pertences da família.
articles.summary: Após ataque de piratas no Amazonas, moradores de Coari relatam agressões e roubos; vídeo mostra família escondida na mata para fugir de criminosos.
articles.body:
Moradores da comunidade São Francisco da Boca do Codajás Mirim, em Coari, no interior do Amazonas, se esconderam em uma área de mata após um ataque de criminosos durante a madrugada de quarta-feira (4). Segundo relatos das vítimas, o grupo invadiu casas, roubou pertences, agrediu moradores e fez ameaças. Pelo menos quatro pessoas teriam sido levadas como reféns.

Nesta quinta-feira (5), a Secretaria de Estado de Segurança Pública do Amazonas (SSP-AM) informou que as pessoas levadas durante a ação já retornaram à comunidade e estão em segurança. A pasta também informou que reforçou o policiamento na região para localizar os suspeitos.

Um vídeo gravado na manhã de quarta-feira e obtido pelo g1 mostra uma mulher com os filhos em meio à mata. Ela relata que precisou passar a noite no local depois que os criminosos invadiram sua casa e levaram os pertences da família.

Nas imagens, as crianças aparecem dormindo no chão, enquanto um homem improvisa uma proteção contra mosquitos. Abalada, a mulher conta que só conseguiu deixar o esconderijo ao amanhecer.

"Os piratas atacaram lá em casa, ontem à noite. Passei a noite no mato com os meus filhos. Meus filhos estão dormindo no mato. Amanhecemos o dia aqui no mato, porque eles levaram tudo o que era nosso, não sobrou nada", relatou aos prantos.

Em áudios enviados por moradores a um policial militar e obtidos pelo g1 , as vítimas contam que passaram por momentos de violência e medo.

Uma delas afirma que, em outro ataque, os criminosos levaram um rádio de comunicação, um motor e um bote. Os relatos também apontam que moradores foram agredidos fisicamente e ameaçados pelos invasores.

Segundo as vítimas, os criminosos proibiram os moradores de registrar a ocorrência na Base Fluvial Arpão 2, localizada no rio Solimões, próximo a Coari. Ainda de acordo com os relatos, o grupo ameaçou voltar e matar os moradores caso eles procurassem as autoridades.

Além dos roubos e das agressões, os moradores relatam prejuízos à atividade pesqueira da comunidade.

Segundo os áudios, os invasores retiraram peixes e levaram equipamentos usados pelos trabalhadores, incluindo embarcações e aparelhos de comunicação.

Em nota divulgada nesta quinta-feira (5), a SSP-AM informou que mobilizou 14 policiais militares para atender à ocorrência. O grupo conta com oito agentes da Base Fluvial Arpão 2 e apoio de uma lancha blindada.

A operação é realizada em conjunto com os batalhões da Polícia Militar de Coari e Codajás. As equipes intensificaram o patrulhamento nos rios próximos à comunidade e fazem buscas para localizar os suspeitos.

A secretaria informou ainda que o reforço no policiamento continuará nos próximos dias para garantir a segurança dos moradores e evitar novos ataques.

A SSP-AM também afirmou que as bases fluviais do estado contribuíram para a apreensão de mais de 50,6 toneladas de drogas entre 2020 e outubro de 2026.

articles.title: A Massachusetts couple renovated a home gifted by the wife's parents using more than $1.5 million from his parents; after divorce, a court revived the dispute over who owed the money
articles.summary: A Massachusetts divorce, a renovated home and a disputed loan of more than $1.5 million came to a head on 11 August 2026, when the First Circuit Court of
articles.body: A Massachusetts divorce, a renovated home and a disputed loan of more than $1.5 million came to a head on 11 August 2026, when the First Circuit Court of Appeals revived a fight between a divorced wife and her former in-laws. Her husband’s parents funded the renovation of a property gifted by her parents, then recorded the money as a loan. A family court awarded her the home after the couple’s divorce, yet a trust holding the parents’ claim sought a sheriff’s sale of her ex-husband’s share, and the appeals court ordered fresh findings on whether the debt was genuine.How a gifted property in Tyringham became a renovation project financed by the husband’s parentsAccording to the First Circuit Court of Appeals ruling in the Cosel and Wendt case, also published in full by FindLaw, Molly Cosel and William Wendt, known as Will, married in 2014. Around the birth of their second child, Molly’s parents deeded a parcel in Tyringham, in western Massachusetts, to the couple as tenants by the entirety, a form of joint ownership for married partners. They planned to renovate one structure and build another, partly as a family home and partly as a studio for Will’s photography career. Will’s parents, Bill and Dalia Wendt, first paid through gifts. Those ran out by November 2017, and from February 2018 they supplied further money, which the court calls the Disputed Funds.Default judgment against the husband and a lien on his share came without notice to his wifeThe marriage began to deteriorate in 2019, and the loan paperwork followed. Will signed a promissory note. Molly did not. Until then, the money carried no interest rate or repayment timeline, though Bill, Dalia and the family accountant each said it was always a loan. Molly moved out temporarily and filed for divorce in February 2020.In November 2020, the parents sued Will alone in the Massachusetts Superior Court. He did not appear, speak to a lawyer or offer a defence, so the court entered a default judgment in December 2020. A writ of execution followed, and the sheriff’s department recorded it at the registry of deeds, creating a judgment lien. Molly was not a party to that suit.A family court found the note created a sham obligation and made the husband solely responsibleIn July 2022, the Family Court’s divorce decree ordered Will to transfer his interest to Molly, required her to pay him $250,000, and made Will alone responsible for the note to the extent it was a legal obligation. The Massachusetts Appeals Court upheld the decree and noted that the Family Court was not plainly wrong to find the note created a sham obligation. The Family Court had also accepted that it could not rule on the parents’ rights under the note, so the decree did not cancel the default judgment.The parents then assigned that judgment to a 2022 family trust bearing the husband’s name, with the couple’s children as beneficiaries and another son, Geoffrey Wendt, as trustee. A sheriff’s sale of Will’s half interest was noticed for 16 September 2022. Molly sued on 19 August 2022 to stop it, and the Wendts, who lived in Indiana, moved the case to federal court. The district court granted her summary judgment, holding that the divorce wiped out the creditor’s interest and that the money was not spent on necessaries, a legal term for certain household expenses.Missing loan terms and unexplained repayment plans kept the question of a genuine loan aliveThe appeals court affirmed in part, reversed in part and vacated in part. It vacated the divorce ruling because the district court had predicted an unsettled question of Massachusetts law while facts that could make it unnecessary remained undecided. Molly, the judges held, was not a party to the default suit, so she was free to challenge the loan’s use against her property. A sham loan, or a scheme to burden a marital asset, could not be enforced against her.The facts pointed both ways. The money became a loan only after the parents learned of the marital trouble; Bill acknowledged that no terms existed before the note, and neither he nor Will could reasonably explain how Will, on a limited income, would repay the sum. The judges called the family’s legal manoeuvres “eyebrow-raising”. But Bill, Dalia and the accountant testified that it was always a loan, which left a dispute for the lower court to resolve.Renovations, a Viking stove and social status, the second dispute over what counts as a necessityMassachusetts law makes both spouses liable for debts incurred for necessaries furnished to either spouse or their family. The term is not limited to food and clothing and, depending on social standing, could cover furniture and even a fur coat. The district court called the renovations high-end improvements, but the appeals court found three factual disputes.One was which work the Disputed Funds paid for: a driveway, a septic system, a Viking stove and a Sub-Zero refrigerator, with the timing unclear. Another was social status. Molly said she was a schoolteacher and Will an aspiring photographer, with a combined income below $180,000. Will described them as multimillionaires planning million-dollar renovations. The third was how to measure the spending against that standing.The ruling’s bottom line, if the loan fails against the wife, the lawsuit ends in her favourThe judges rejected the trust’s argument that Molly’s move away meant the property was no longer her principal residence, finding that she intended to return. They also rejected Molly’s argument that the domestic relations exception, a rule limiting federal courts in certain family matters, barred the trust’s counterclaims, since neither the trust nor the Wendts were parties to the divorce.You use AI every day. articles.title: John Frieda, celebrity hairstylist and haircare mogul, dead at 75
articles.summary: Hairstylist to the stars John Frieda, counted Madonna and Princess Diana among his clients.
articles.body: John Frieda, the celebrity hairstylist whose eponymous product range — its beloved Frizz Ease serum, especially — proved a commercial sensation, has died aged 75. The British entrepreneur, who counted Madonna and Princess Diana among his clients, died “peacefully” and “surrounded by his family,” according to a statement posted to his Instagram by his London salon on Wednesday. “His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us,” the statement added, describing Frieda as “a true icon of the hair industry.” His stepdaughter Agnelli Lagrange also confirmed the news on social media, where she called him “the best man to ever exist.” Neither statement specified a cause of death. The son of a hairdresser (and the grandson of a barber), Frieda was born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951. He started going by the name John after joining London’s famous House of Leonard, because the salon already employed an Alan. From the late 1960s, as assistant to the salon’s owner Leonard Lewis, Frieda helped style hair for some of the era’s biggest names, including Mick Jagger, Twiggy and Jackie Kennedy Onassis. In 1976, then only in his mid-20s, Frieda opened his own salon in London’s West End. That year, he invented the “Purdey” — a chic take on a bowl cut — for actor Joanna Lumley, who famously wore the style in the TV spy series “The New Avengers.” Frieda expanded his celebrity clientele in the 1980s, working with stars including Princess Diana, Madonna and Paul McCartney, as well as styling for television and fashion editorials. He opened a second location in London’s exclusive Mayfair neighborhood, but his ambitions went beyond the salon business. “Although it was a lot of fun and very interesting — and I felt that I’d had a certain amount of success and done very, very well — I wasn’t really challenged enough,” he told CNN in 2007, recalling his early career. “Particularly, I didn’t feel I was mentally challenged enough. It was at that moment when I decided that I would start my own product range.” In 1989, Frieda teamed up with beauty entrepreneur Gail Federici to launch a consumer haircare line, John Frieda Professional Hair Care. Having successfully debuted the company’s signature product, Frizz Ease, in the UK, the pair launched the range in 1990. Designed to be applied to wet hair after shampooing, the anti-frizz serum’s promise was straightforward: “Frizz Ease turns dry frizzy hair into smooth shiny hair quickly,” Frieda told American viewers in a 1993 commercial. It flew off the shelves, effectively launching a new category of haircare products that did not previously exist. By then living in the US, Frieda expanded his salon business throughout the 1990s, opening locations in New York and LA. His eponymous brand also used the success of Frizz Ease to expand its offering, including products aimed at specific hair colors — like the popular Sheer Blonde line, launched in 1998. In 2002, Frieda and Federici sold their company to the Japanese chemical and cosmetics firm Kao Corporation for $450 million. Last year, the UK’s Sunday Times Rich List listed Frieda’s wealth at £150 million ($202 million). Frieda married Scottish singer Lulu, with whom he shares a son, in 1977. He is also survived by his second wife Avery Agnelli, the widow of Fiat heir Giovanni Agnelli, and their two children.

articles.title: Italian chef fired from Queensland restaurant after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
articles.summary: He had told his employer, an Australian restaurant, that pineapple on pizza was "offensive" to Italian culture.
articles.body:
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".

Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.

Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".

The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.

In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".

It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.

He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".

The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.

On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.

Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".

The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.

Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.

However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that process, the tribunal heard.

He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.

The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".

The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.

On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".

Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".

The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on its menu.

articles.title: Canford Heath nature reserve fire covers seven hectares
articles.summary: A wildfire on Canford Heath nature reserve spread rapidly due to high winds on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
Firefighters are tackling flare-ups from a heathland fire at a nature reserve that covers about seven hectares (17 acres).

The blaze on Canford Heath near Poole broke out on Wednesday at about 20:00 GMT with about 45 firefighters from across Dorset and Hampshire initially sent in 14 firefighting appliances.

Dorset & Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service said flames had spread rapidly due to high winds. It said crews in numerous off-road appliances, along with a drone, were working to manage flare-ups and hotspots.

Residents are being urged to avoid the area and keep windows and doors closed due to the smoke.

The 344-hectare Canford Heath is a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest.

It is home to dragonflies, damselflies, Dartford warblers, nightjars and all six species of British reptile.

articles.title: Herbert Blomstedt, who headed San Francisco Symphony, dies at 99
articles.summary: Herbert Blomstedt, who headed the San Francisco Symphony from 1985-95 and led orchestras in Scandinavia and Germany during a career over seven decades, has died.
articles.body: Herbert Blomstedt, who headed the San Francisco Symphony from 1985-95 and led orchestras in Scandinavia and Germany during a career over seven decades, died on Wednesday. He was 99. Blomstedt died at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden, according to his management agency, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig. His final performance was on May 15 with the San Francisco Symphony at Davies Hall, when he entered the stage in a wheelchair and struggled to get through Gustav Mahler’s Ninth Symphony, which halted for several minutes during the third movement. He was replaced for concerts the following two days and canceled future scheduled appearances this year. “An an extraordinary role model,” Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra music director Manfred Honeck said. “One of the greatest conductors and a beacon of humanity.” Blomstedt had performances scheduled into 2027, including with the Vienna Philharmonic next June, just shy of what would have been his 100th birthday. “Until the very end, we had hoped to celebrate his 100th birthday with a concert together,” Vienna Philharmonic chairman Daniel Froschauer said. Blomstedt was a Seventh-day Adventist who refused to conduct rehearsals on Friday nights and Saturdays because of the Sabbath but would lead performances on those days because he considered himself a preacher of music. “Every bar, every note is shared by us, and it’s a very intense communication,” he said of his conducting during an interview with “CBS Sunday Morning” broadcast last year. “It’s like intense sex.” He won Grammy Awards for recordings with the San Francisco Symphony of Carl Orff’s “Carmina Burana” in 1993 and of Johannes Brahms’ “Ein Deutsches Requiem” in 1996. “My mission is to bring good music to as many people as possible,” he said in an interview posted in 2020 by the DW Music YouTube channel. “It makes you think differently. You gave a more keen feeling for proportions and beauty.” Blomstedt was principal conductor of the Norrköping Symphony Orchestra in Sweden from 1954-63, music director of the Oslo Philharmonic from 1962–68, principal conductor of the Danish Radio Symphony from 1967-77 and the Swedish Radio Symphony from 1977-82 and then became chief conductor of the Staatskapelle Dresden and Semperoper in Germany from 1975-85. “Almost like turning an electrical switch for me,” he added. “When I hear the sound, it transforms me. I’m in heaven.” Esa-Pekka Salonen, who led the San Francisco Symphony from 2020-25, said during an interview with London’s Philharmonia Orchestra in 2021 that he asked Blomstedt how he was filled with joy that orchestras responded to. “I refuse to have any stress,” Salonen recalled Blomstedt telling him. “I only do things I absolutely love. I only conduct music that matters to me and I only work with people that I like and in some cases love.” After leaving San Francisco, Blomstedt was principal conductor of Hamburg’s NDR Symphony Orchestra from 1996-98 and music director of the Leipzig Gewanhaus Orchestra from 1998-2005. Born to Swedish parents in Springfield, Massachusetts, on July 11, 1927. His family moved back to Sweden in 1929 and he attended Stockholm’s Royal Academy of Music and Uppsala University. He studied under Igor Markevitch, then with Jean Morel at The Juilliard School. When his scholarship at Juilliard was about to expire, he showed up without an appointment at Leonard Bernstein’s apartment at The Osborne across from Carnegie Hall, rang the doorbell and left a half-hour later with a scholarship to study with Bernstein at the Tanglewood Music Center in Lenox, Massachusetts. Blomstedt was impressed with Bernstein’s musicianship but disliked his exuberant podium mannerisms. Blomstedt won the Koussevitzky Conducting Prize in 1953, made his professional debut with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra in 1954 and won the Salzburg Conducting Competition in 1955. He married his wife, the former Waltraud Petersen, in 1955, and she died in 2003. He is survived by four daughters and seven grandchildren.

articles.title: France holds new strikes and protests as unions demand immediate answers
articles.summary: Five of France's unions join a wave of strikes and protests in a national day of action.
articles.body:
Protests are taking place across France after five unions launched a national day of strike action, joining high school students and demonstrators criticising the rising cost of living.

More than 250,000 people had taken to the streets in almost 70 towns and cities by 13:00 (12:00 GMT) on Thursday, and that was "just the start", said Sophie Binet of the CGT union.

The unions have vowed to take the wave of protests that began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools) "to the next level".

They have since spread to include workers and the so-called "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 70,000 police were being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.

Some unrest has been reported in the cities of Lyon and Rennes.

A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in central Lyon, as hundreds of people belonging to the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.

Meanwhile, there were clashes in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march.

The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, announcing more than 250 separate actions as part of their campaign for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protect public services.

Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.

Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.

Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.

A coalition of unions has urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently €12.31 (£10) an hour.

The head of the CFDT union, Marylise Léon, complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase: "We are asking for a net increase of €100 a month."

The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.

The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycées, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.

"Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.

Large numbers were expected on the streets, especially in the capital, and the CFDT leader said she would be happy if 800,000 people turned out. Those numbers were last seen on 17 October.

Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.

'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation

France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police

Union leaders have complained that recent marches have been kept away from the centre of Paris, because of violence that broke out in towns and cities on 17 October and led to more than 2,000 stores being looted and historic buildings being set on fire.

Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the Élysée Palace, and the prime minister's residence at Hôtel Matignon.

Instead, the march was set to follow another central route from Place de la République to Place de la Nation. The CFDT union complained that getting court approval for the route only on Wednesday evening made organising the march more difficult.

The last big mobilisation at the weekend passed off with relatively little violence, and the interior minister said the police deployment would be on a similar scale on Thursday. Nuñez has spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

articles.title: European flights targeted by 'malicious hoax' bomb threats for second time this week
articles.summary: At least 18 flights across Europe are affected in what the UK government calls a "malicious hoax threat".
articles.body:
At least 18 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats - the second such incident this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax".

Flights bound for Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected, including an Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome which was forced to divert to a military air base in France.

Italian fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome, where it landed as scheduled. No explosives have been found during searches. EasyJet said two of its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by Czech police after arriving in Prague as a "precautionary measure".

It is not clear if the incidents are related.

UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."

She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".

A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.

The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.

The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".

They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.

These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.

The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:

Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible".

Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria

Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft

Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found

Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets

No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said

Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports"

A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported

Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight

Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded"

Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.

Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.

On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."

Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing and saw one touch down behind the aircraft.

After landing at the Évreux-Fauville air base in Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat.

Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs.

The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome.

Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents.

A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said.

He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".

Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real".

He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel.

Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion".

Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches.

On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

articles.title: Israel extends detention of Palestinian journalist Abed Abou Shhadeh
articles.summary: Rights group says the journalist’s arrest over an interview with Azmi Bishara is an attempt to silence Palestinians.
articles.body:
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Palestinian journalist and political activist Abed Abou Shhadeh who was arrested this week.

Abou Shhadeh was detained after Israeli security forces raided his home in Jaffa overnight on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Tel Aviv Magistrate’s Court ruled that he will remain in custody until Sunday, November 8.

Abou Shhadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, hosts the al-Midan podcast for the Arab48 website and appeared as an analyst on Al Jazeera during coverage of the recent Israeli election.

Police had requested an eight-day extension to his detention on suspicion of “contact with a foreign agent”. The legal rights group Adalah, which is part of his defence team, said it would appeal.

Speaking on Al Jazeera, Adalah founder Hassan Jabareen said Abou Shhadeh had been charged with receiving money from foreign agents in order to support Arab-Israeli voters. Jabareen dismissed the charges as fabricated.

“There is no evidence that [Abou Shhadeh] received money from anyone,” he told Al Jazeera. “They searched his house and found nothing.”

About 15 security officers, some of them masked, had raided Abou Shhadeh’s home overnight on Tuesday, confiscating electronic devices and books in front of his two children.

Arab48 reported that police initially refused to tell his family where he was being held. His lawyer later discovered he was detained at a Shin Bet intelligence facility in Petah Tikva.

“All of this story [is] part of the campaign by the head of [the Shin Bet] and [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu who want to show that Arab voters in Israel are not kosher, are illegal,” Jabareen said.

No party emerged as the winner in Israel’s election last week, with Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, now needing to form a coalition with smaller parties to be able to govern. Arab-led parties made record gains this year, making their collective alliance a candidate for coalition partner.

“The motive behind all of this is the election,” Jabareen told Al Jazeera. “It’s to show that Arab voters and political parties are illegal, so they can’t make a coalition with Eisonkot.”

Israeli media reported that Abou Shhadeh was arrested after taking part in an interview in Qatar with the Palestinian intellectual Azmi Bishara. Abou Shhadeh’s lawyers say his interrogation focused solely on the interview he conducted with the former Knesset member.

“This is not a criminal investigation, it is a campaign to silence Palestinian journalists and political activists,” Adalah lawyer Hadeel Abu Salih said in a statement.

“The police are sending a message to the entire Palestinian public in Israel: Even a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a detention cell.”

According to Adalah, police raised no allegations against Abou Shhadeh other than the interview, which covered the Israeli election campaign and Palestinians, and remains publicly available.

At the hearing, the defence argued that Bishara, a former head of the Arab-Israei party Balad, is not a “foreign agent” and that interviewing him cannot give rise to suspicion of a criminal offence.

According to the Israeli daily Israel Hayom, lawyers also told the court that Abou Shhadeh had worked as a journalist for about six years and conducted the interview as part of the work. They said it was “not a secret meeting” and that investigators already held Abou Shhadeh phone and computer, so there was no real risk of him obstructing the investigation.

Dozens of Palestinian and Jewish activists protested outside the court on Wednesday to demand his release.

Rights advocates have described the arrest as part of a campaign of intimidation against Palestinian citizens of Israel following the election.

David Zini, chief of the Shin Bet, Israel’s security agency, has reportedly sought to question Arab party leaders Mansour Abbas, Ahmad Tibi and Sami Abu Shehadeh , the Balad leader and a relative of the detained journalist.

articles.title: A month after Yemen government offensive began, war of attrition takes hold
articles.summary: The Houthis suffer losses but also inflict pain on government forces and Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – When news broke on October 5 that Yemen’s internationally recognised government was launching a major new offensive to take control of territories held by Houthi fighters, Mohammed Ahmed began to prepare for the worst.

Sanaa has been under Houthi control since late 2014 after the Houthis seized the capital city in the initial phase of a civil war that has ebbed and flowed for more than a decade.

But when it announced Operation Dawn of Yemen , the new offensive, last month, Yemeni government forces, backed by a Saudi Arabia-led coalition, declared they would aim to retake control of all parts of the country held by the Houthis, including Sanaa.

“A state of worry and uncertainty overwhelmed my family and me,” Ahmed, a 40-year-old resident of Sanaa, said.

Ahmed was not concerned about which side would emerge victorious. Instead, he feared the consequences of hostilities near or inside Yemen’s most densely populated city.

A month after the operation began, Ahmed’s anxiety has eased as Sanaa remains largely calm, apart from recurring air strikes.

Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have scored territorial gains in other provinces, including Taiz and Lahij in southern Yemen, where fighting has not ceased.

But while Yemenis such as Ahmed said the initial momentum surrounding Dawn of Yemen has faded, experts and researchers view the operation as marking a new phase in a war of attrition that shows no signs of easing.

Turki al-Goblan, head of the Saudi Daimumah Center for Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Houthis have survived in previous years by adapting to strikes and leveraging complex geography, clandestine supply and concealment networks, and the use of civilians as human shields.

That survival strategy is now under stress. The Dawn of Yemen offensive has “dealt a blow to the three pillars of this strategy”, al-Goblan said.

The first pillar, according to him, is the fuel and supply system, which keeps Houthi combat vehicles moving, transports ammunition and delivers reinforcements. Second, the operation has hit the Houthis in the maritime areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the western coast, which serve as outlets through which alternative external supply routes pass. Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea and is a major waterway through which Saudi Arabia exports its oil and Asian economies, such as China, ship commodities to Europe.

Third, some of the tribes surrounding Sanaa have begun declaring mobilisation in support of the internationally recognised Yemeni government, undermining the Iran-backed Houthis’ reliance on them.

“When these three pillars are targeted simultaneously, the question shifts from the scale of losses to the ability to replenish them,” al-Goblan added.

He argued that the pace of attrition has exceeded the Houthis’ ability to recover.

“Attrition ceases to be the opposite of a decisive victory and becomes the means of achieving it as repeated losses translate into an accumulating inability to sustain the fight. This is the scenario I consider more likely.”

Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have taken control of much of northern and western Yemen. Since then, the conflict has remained unresolved.

Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Yemeni Abaad Studies and Research Center, said the Dawn of Yemen pushed the Houthis to move their forces and their military capabilities, exposing the group to deadly attacks.

“Many of the Houthi field commanders and hundreds of fighters have been killed in air strikes, especially in Taiz and Yemen’s western coast. While the killing of these fighters has not stopped Houthi territorial gains, these gains can be short-lived if the government airpower and ground fighters keep launching coordinated military attacks,” Mohammed said.

Last month, the Yemeni government said its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Late last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5. The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles and drones daily into Saudi Arabia too, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.

“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he said.

Iran sees the Houthis as a source of strategic leverage, al-Jeddawy noted. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia seeks to curb the group’s military capabilities and prevent it from threatening vital maritime routes, particularly Bab al-Mandeb.

“The growing intensity of the fighting, the scale of the losses they are prepared to absorb and their willingness to climb the escalation ladder suggest an increasingly zero-sum approach,” al-Jeddawy added.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the total number of attacks by the Saudi-led coalition, including air strikes, in Yemen has reached 3,939 since the latest escalation began.

On Monday, the country’s Presidential Leadership Council reaffirmed its commitment to the Dawn of Yemen and its objectives, namely ending the Houthi “coup”, restoring state institutions and extending the state’s authority over its entire territory.

Colonel Wadah al-Dubaish, spokesperson for the government-aligned Joint Forces on Yemen’s West Coast, told Al Jazeera the Houthis have lately expanded their military gains in Taiz; however, the price of such a move is extremely high.

“The group’s expansion has been a big adventure. What the Houthis have lost over the past month is more than their losses over the past years combined.”

Yemeni government forces said they had reclaimed control of the Taiz governorate’s Dhubab district and key positions near Bab al-Mandeb.

Al-Dubaish indicated that the Houthis capitalised on ceasefires over the past decade that offered the group more time to prepare and mobilise for war.

“The lesson is clear: The group threatens all factions in Yemen, and efforts should be united to confront this threat,” he said.

Yemen’s government said on Sunday that its forces recaptured military positions and strategic heights east of al-Hazm, the capital of the northern governorate of al-Jawf.

The Houthis’ resilient missile capability

Since the start of the Dawn of Yemen, neither Yemen’s government-controlled territories nor Saudi Arabia has been safe from Houthi missile attacks.

The group has repeatedly launched missiles, occasionally causing damage, deaths and injuries. One of its latest missile attacks killed at least 70 government security recruits in Shabwah.

Al-Jeddawy said the continued attacks showed that the Houthis retain a functioning and resilient missile capability.

“But the more important question is not simply how many missiles they still possess; it is the scale and nature of the external support they continue to receive – whether in intelligence, targeting assistance, components, technical expertise or weapons replenishment,” he said.

The timing and volume of the attacks, together with the precision and damage achieved in some strikes, point to a wider support system that goes beyond the Houthis’ capabilities in isolation, according to al-Jeddawy.

Al-Goblan, however, interpreted the Houthis’ continued missile and drone attacks differently, arguing that they do not necessarily demonstrate military strength or a coherent operational strategy as the Dawn of Yemen continues.

“Rather, it may represent an attempt to compensate for declining ground manoeuvrability through long-range firepower. It may also be an effort to preserve cohesion across fronts and create a political impact and an illusion of maintaining the initiative,” al- Goblan said.

articles.title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
articles.summary: A consultation will consider fines and other ways to clamp down on dangerous e-bike riders.
articles.body:
People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.

Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.

They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.

It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.

A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.

According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year.

Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.

While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.

Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.

The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines - for this type of behaviour.

The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.

The consultation will last for eight weeks after which the government will draw up legislation to implement the changes.

'Dumped e-scooters force blind people into road'

Red light jumping cyclists offered film over fine

'Our lives will never be the same again after Lime bike crash'

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government wanted e-bike schemes to "grow in popularity" but acknowledged they were "causing a little bit of nuisance at the moment".

Asked how punishments for dangerous cycling could be enforced, Alexander said licensing rules could allow for fines but added: "What you can't do is legislate for every eventuality, you can't legislate for idiots."

"The police enforce the rules of the road to stop cyclists when they are behaving recklessly but police have got a lot on their plate so individuals have to take some responsibility," she added.

Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.

Mike Wordingham from the Royal National Institute for the Blind said 92% of blind and partially sighted people had been forced to walk into roads due to e-bikes blocking pavements.

He welcomed the government's announced but warned that tackling rider behaviour would be "difficult" and said a locally-led approach shouldn't lead to "a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them".

articles.title: Developer says £1.2bn Norwich data centre will boost city
articles.summary: It is being met with fierce opposition but the developer insists the city will see benefits.
articles.body:
A developer has defended plans for a £1.2bn data centre on the edge of a city, insisting it will benefit the area despite thousands of objections.

Matt Bartram, chief executive of Norwich Apex Ltd, said the scheme opposite Tesco Harford Bridge on the A140 could help turn Norwich into a "tech hub" amid a booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI).

His team wants to create one of the UK's "greenest data centres" despite campaigners claiming it would have "terrible consequences" for neighbouring wildlife sites.

If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027, with the data centre expected to be operational by 2028.

Bartram added: "I doubt Norfolk will see many opportunities like this again.

"This is something that will be a positive thing for Norwich. We will develop this in a responsible manner.

"Data centres are becoming increasingly important to our everyday lives, supporting everything from healthcare and financial services to the development of artificial intelligence."

Plans have been lodged with South Norfolk Council for the project in Keswick and a decision on the scheme is expected to be made early next year.

But Bartram said its ecological assessments predicted that the data centre "is not expected to have any discernible impact" on the surrounding nature reserves.

He added the site would use a closed-loop water cooling system which meant that once filled, no more water would be needed.

Mitigation measures would be implemented to prevent noise generated by the 72 cooling units on its roof increasing current background noise from the nearby roads, he said.

Bartram added: "We recognise that a development of this scale raises legitimate questions about its environmental impact and what it means for neighbouring communities.

"Our ambition is to deliver a development that benefits the region economically while setting high standards for environmental responsibility."

The Norwich Apex data centre would need 150MW of power to run it and hoped to utilise wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.

While significant, the scale of the site pales in comparison to another planned in Norfolk.

The Longmarsh Green Energy project planned for farmland near King's Lynn would need 1.3GW to power it - and developers want to create one of the biggest solar farms in the country to supply energy for it.
