articles.title: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.summary: Bomb threats forced the diversion of a series of flights across Europe on Thursday, just two days after at least seven flights received similar threats.
articles.body:
• Bomb threats forced the diversion of more than a dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, the latest in a string of incidents disrupting airspace. Several authorities have said no devices have been found.

• Four of the flight diversions were in the Czech Republic. The bomb threats were made in an anonymous email and other airports received the email too, a representative of the Václav Havel Airport in Prague told CNN .

• A company linked to Rome’s airport received an email from a group purporting to be anti-feminist and calling itself the Male State that claimed there were bombs on two flights. But it is unconfirmed who was behind the wave of threats and the EU says it is too early to say they are linked.

Passengers at Rome Fiumicino airport said they would go ahead with their travels on Thursday, after bomb threats that turned out to be false impacted two flights bound for the Italian capital.

One affected flight from Dublin was diverted to Normandy in France, whilst the other, from Helsinki, was escorted safely into Rome airport by Italian air force fighter jets.

The airport operator ADR conducted searches and said there was no threat, according to Reuters.

Watch the video to hear how passengers are reacting.

While it remains unclear who is responsible for the spate of bomb threats across Europe this week, one aviation expert said he is looking closely at Russia.

“From a geopolitical view, I’m thinking, you always have to think about the scenario of hybrid warfare, where a country in this way — today we are looking at Russia, right? — is attacking us on multiple fronts, from railways to supermarkets to blood banks, most recently,” Eric Schouten, head of the aviation security ⁠group Dyami, told Reuters.

“The energy sector, the internet sector, and the aviation sector are among those,” he added.

Russia has recently been accused by Denmark, Poland and Romania of causing disruption through hybrid attacks - hostile action that targets and destabilizes an adversary through a blend of non-military tactics and cyber assaults on essential infrastructure.

The unconventional mixture of techniques used in such an attack makes it difficult to trace back to a single actor, he said.

Denmark, Poland and Romania are also among the nations impacted by Thursday’s disruptions, and Schouten pointed out that those affected have supported Ukraine during Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Earlier Thursday, CNN affiliate SKYTG24 published an email from an anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” which appeared to reveal the origin of a false bomb threat claims made regarding two flights bound for an airport in Rome.

The International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, a Netherlands-based think tank, said “The Male State” was created in Russia in 2016.

“It transition from being one of the most notorious misogynist movements in Russia to one of the main online supporters and promoters of the war in Ukraine,” the report said .

Russia has denied engaging in hybrid warfare.

Passengers and crew on at least 14 planes have been impacted by bomb threats in Europe today, with multiple flights rerouted and some having to be escorted by fighter jets.

All the threats have so far proven false, and there’s no clear indication who’s behind them, but they are causing considerable disruption.

Here’s a running CNN tally of flights affected, based on information from airlines and regional officials:

France: One flight handled by the Irish carrier, Aer Lingus, landed in Normandy, northern France after leaving Dublin for Rome, Italy.

Italy: Two flights en route from Thessaloniki, northern Greece and Porto, northern Portugal landed safely in Milan where checks found no explosives. One flight from Helsinki was escorted by Italian air force jets and safely landed in Rome.

Bulgaria: Two flights – each traveling from Madrid in Spain and Copenhagen in Denmark – were diverted to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. Another plane that set off from London, in the UK, was diverted to Plovdiv, just southeast of Sofia.

Czech Republic: Four flights landed in Václav Havel Airport in the capital, Prague.

Belgium: One flight handled by LOT Polish Airlines departed from Warsaw, according to Reuters, before being diverted to Brussels, in Belgium, local media said.

Romania: One Wizz Air flight departing from Rome landed in the Romanian capital, Bucharest.

Austria: Another Wizz Air flight from Milan landed in Vienna, Austria.

Matthew Bojarsky’s LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Paris was taxiing to the runway when the pilot announced it had been cancelled for safety reasons.

Passengers were told the plane would wait at the end of the runway for “some officers,” he told CNN, after posting a video on X that shows men in military fatigues outside the plane.

Eventually the flight, one of more than a dozen to face bomb threats on Thursday, was continued on a different plane.

“We were moved into a hall, then waited for four hours,” Bojarsky said. “We got the information from the news, the pilot said it was ‘safety protocol’.”

Officials at the Madrid-Barajas Airport in Spain’s capital received a “bomb threat” naming three flights on Thursday, airport operator AENA said.

Law enforcement teams carried out an assessment “and the relevant security checks” and found nothing on board, a spokesperson for AENA told CNN.

An anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” emailed bomb threats to a logistics company working with Rome Fiumicino Airport on Thursday naming two flights bound for the Italian capital.

The email, first published by CNN Affiliate SkyTG24, made the false claim that “explosive devices” had been placed on two flights – one from Helsinki and another from Dublin. A spokesperson for the airport confirmed to CNN the screenshot was authentic.

“You’re all complicit in a criminal plot, we want to annihilate you for this,” the memo read in Italian. “We, the fighters of the Male State, with our actions will leave a mark on history. Your feminist regime will never forget it.”

Earlier on Thursday , Italian air force fighter jets escorted the Finnair flight from Helsinki safely into Rome airport. A second flight from Dublin to Rome, operated by the Irish airline, Aer Lingus, was diverted to Normandy, northern France.

The email went to Aviapartner, a Belgium-based logistics company providing luggage services to the Rome airport.

The email alias appeared to be linked to the municipality of the Colombian capital Bogotá, whose mayor Luis Fernando Galan told CNN his team was working to establish what happened.

“It could be the account was hacked, we’ve had several of them before,” Galan told CNN.

The EU transport commissioner said it is “too early” to determine whether the bomb threats that caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their scheduled destination across Europe this week are connected.

“It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked,” Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a statement released Thursday, “National investigations remain ongoing.”

The commissioner said that the situation is being closely monitored, and that the department is “in contact with the affected member states and the European Aviation Safety Agency.”

“The EU-level information sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security,” it added.

The commissioner said any threat against civilians is “unacceptable,” and said all relevant bodies have been liaising to ensure aviation safety and security is not compromised.

While no explosive devices have yet been found following bomb threats, the motivation behind the reports remains unclear.

The UK’s transport minister says the bomb threats that have caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their destinations are a “malicious hoax.”

Speaking to British media, Heidi Alexander said that the disrupted flights had triggered “established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats, and that’s what these threats have been.”

While the minister insisted that the British government is taking the threats seriously, she added “we understand these have been malicious hoax threats.”

At least 14 flights have been impacted by the threats Thursday. No explosives have yet been found.

Bulgaria’s transport authorities are the latest to confirm that their inspections found no issues on any of the three aircraft that were the subject of this morning’s bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights to Sofia from Madrid and Copenhagen respectively landed safely at their destination after the bomb threats.

Another Ryanair flight from London was diverted to Plovdiv, southeast of the capital, following a threat.

“Upon landing, the necessary inspections were carried out in accordance with the applicable procedures and no issues were identified,” a spokesperson for Bulgaria’s transport ministry told CNN Thursday.

Both airports are operating as normal and the airline arranged transportation to Sofia from Plovdiv for diverted passengers.

A representative of the Václav Havel Airport in Prague told CNN the threats it received about bombs being placed on four flights were made in an anonymous email.

A Czech Police spokesperson told CNN the email was addressed to the airport, adding that similar emails were sent to other airports in Europe.

The Prague airport immediately contacted emergency services and convened a meeting of its crisis committee.

Neither the airport representative nor the police said which language the email was written in.

In another incident, almost 200 passengers were evacuated from a Wizz Air flight after it landed safely in Bucharest, Romania, Thursday morning local time following a bomb threat, bringing the total to at least 14.

Romania’s intelligence agency said the aircraft, which departed from Milan, has been checked and no explosives found, Reuters reported.

Two planes from European cities were diverted to Malpensa Airport in Milan, in Italy on Thursday following bomb threats, according to airport officials.

Italian border police were carrying out “bomb checks” on both planes, the airport said in a statement. One Aegean Airlines flight had set off from Thessaloniki, northern Greece, while the other was a Ryanair flight from the city of Porto, northern Portugal.

The Czech National Center against Terrorism, Extremism and Cybercrime, a specialized unit of the Czech Police, is taking over the investigation into the threats made against four airplanes headed to Prague.

Czech authorities are in contact with their international partners, Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said on X.

A plane rerouted a flight from Dublin to Rome following a bomb threat is now at the Evreux air base in Normandy.

The plane “landed safely,” according to the Irish carrier, Aer Lingus.

About 151 passengers and six crew members were “being moved to safety” following the “bomb threat,” the French prime minister’s office said.

There’s no word yet whether there was a bomb on board but other national authorities say the threats they received were hoaxes.

Much is unknown about the latest threats to flights - no one claimed responsibility for the alerts earlier this week and no one has claimed Thursday’s threats either.

But, coming off the back of hackers targeting supermarket fridges, experts say such attacks could serve multiple purposes, from causing disruption to testing authorities’ response.

“These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe,” said Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation.

At least seven flights and one cruise ship received bomb threats across Europe on Tuesday, triggering disruption at airports and causing concern among travelers.

Yet no explosive devices were discovered.

The threat named two flights to the Polish capital Warsaw, two to the Bulgarian capital Sofia, two to the Italian capital Rome and one to the Spanish city of Murcia.

An airport in Warsaw was temporarily closed, the Italian Air Force escorted one flight to Rome, and a cruise ship bound for Israel was halted in Greece while it was searched for bombs.

A Wizz Air-operated flight from Bergamo, Italy, and a Ryanair flight from Dublin both landed safely at their destination of Sofia, where they were inspected and no explosive devices were found.

Meanwhile, in southeastern Spain, segments of the airport in Murcia were cordoned off in response to a bomb threat reported on a Ryanair flight inbound from Manchester, England. After investigation, officials deemed the report a hoax and re-opened the airport.

In Rome, two other Ryanair flights, from Lisbon and Dublin respectively, were also searched following bomb threats - no risk was located on either aircraft.

And in Greece, an explosives detection dog scoured the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship after an unidentified person reported that an explosive device had been fitted to the boat’s hull, Reuters cited authorities as saying. The vessel resumed its voyage after coast guard specialists reported it free of risk.

None of Tuesday’s bomb threats have been claimed by any group, nor has any country suggested where blame might lie.

We’ve just had an update from authorities in the Czech Republic and Italy that no explosives have been found after alerts caused flight diversions.

“The operation at the airport is over, there were no bombs and everyone is safe,” Czech Police said.

Rome Airport also confirmed the operation there is over, with no bombs discovered.

Four aircraft are rerouting to Prague in the Czech Republic after authorities were alerted to a threat over “improvised explosive devices,” national police reported on Thursday.

The Czech Police are liaising with colleagues at the capital’s Václav Havel Airport to “prepare for their landing,” according to a police statement. Officials assess the threat of the bomb being real as “low,” the police statement said, adding that “inspections will be conducted on all aircraft.”

“Nevertheless, we do not underestimate the threat, which is why all necessary security measures have been activated while minimising the possible impact on passengers and airport operations,” the police statement said.

The Air Navigation Services of the Czech Republic said it is “handling the current situation based upon the requirements of the crews and in accordance with regulations.”

The Prague airport is the main airport in the Czech Republic and handled 17.8 million passengers last year.

Bomb threats forced the diversion of a series of flights across Europe on Thursday for a second time this week.

Aer Lingus said a flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy in France as a security precaution.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki was escorted by two Italian air force fighter jets to Rome Fiumicino Airport after a bomb threat on Thursday morning, a spokesperson for the airport told CNN. Bomb checks are still being performed and are being carried out by Italian police.

Bulgarian media reported emergency landings of three aircraft following bomb threats. Two of the aircraft departed from Copenhagen and Madrid, landing safely in the Bulgarian capital of Sofia, Reuters reported, citing local media. A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv in Bulgaria, the reports said.

Reuters also reported that Polish airline LOT had received a suspicious report regarding one of its planes which had departed from Warsaw. It has since landed safely in Brussels, Belgian media reported.

We’ll bring you the latest on this as we get it.

articles.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
articles.summary: The widow of ER creator Michael Crichton argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the 1990s series.
articles.body:
US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.

The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.

Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.

A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.

Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.

"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.

It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.

But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.

The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.

ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.

The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.

Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.

Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.

But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series.

They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs".

Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.

After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".

But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim.

Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".

The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events.

Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."

Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

articles.title: Google HQ refused 54,000-signature petition, campaigners say
articles.summary: Campaigners oppose the development of a large data centre on a wildlife site at Thurrock.
articles.body:
Protesters claim Google's headquarters in London refused a petition of 54,000 signatories worried about the environmental impact of an Essex development.

The tech giant plans to build four data centre buildings, covering 130,500 sqm, and an office building on the former Arena Essex Raceway near Purfleet which closed in 2018 .

The 52 hectares of land became a Local Wildlife Site in 2006 and conservationists said the development would threaten rare bumblebees and endangered broad-leaved cudweed.

Google would not confirm or deny that it refused the petition on Wednesday, but said data centres were "vital" and that the firm was taking its environmental responsibilities "very seriously".

A number of environmental groups claim the development would wipe out more than 80% of its protected habitats, as the site is also home to butterflies and nightingales.

They have called for Google to "search elsewhere", and want it opened up as a green space and the return of the racers.

Jamie Robins, programmes manager at Buglife, said the plan "makes a mockery" of Google's sustainability claims.

"Handing in this petition today is making it clear to Google that their Thurrock Data Centre plans are inappropriate and unwanted," he said.

"During a nature and climate emergency, with our insects in decline, we should be protecting our precious wildlife sites and need powerful companies to lead and make better decisions."

Emily Buttress, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said: "Its loss would be devastating for the local area.

"It would fragment the ecological network even further, putting already at-risk wildlife under an even greater threat."

A Google spokesperson said: "Data centres are vital to the UK, providing the critical infrastructure required to power our digital economy and the online services used by people in every corner of the UK.

"As we work to deliver this critical infrastructure, we share the Essex Wildlife Trust and Buglife's view that development at the former Arena Essex site must be sustainable.

"Our goal is to regenerate the site, bringing long-term investment and jobs to Thurrock while taking our environmental responsibilities very seriously.

"We are working closely with Natural England and ecological experts to guarantee a 10% Biodiversity Net Gain.

"Our proposal also ensures a substantial part of the site is preserved for new public open space, green links, retained habitat, and the long-term enhancement of key woodland corridors."

articles.title: Monty Don prepares for final BBC Gardeners' World episode
articles.summary: The presenter says Friday will be his "very last" Gardeners' World episode after 23 years.
articles.body:
Monty Don will host Gardeners' World for the very last time this week after more than 20 years.

In September, the BBC announced the green-fingered presenter would depart the show at the end of the current series.

In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience", but added: "Now is the right time for a change."

And in an update, published on the Gardeners' World Instagram page, the 71-year-old said Friday (6 November) would be "my very last".

He said: "This Friday will be my very last Gardeners' World. I began 23 years ago.

"But, it's a brilliant programme as ever, and it's been a complete privilege to be part of it.

"So, join me on Friday for the last time."

Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years.

articles.title: Water rescues, evacuations underway as ‘catastrophic flood event’ hits North Georgia and southern Tennessee
articles.summary: Catastrophic flooding is in progress as waterways burst their banks.
articles.body: Homes and businesses are flooded, and water rescues and evacuations are in progress, as historic flooding impacts North Georgia and southern Tennessee. ⛈️☔️Get your forecast and track the storm in the CNN Weather app Flash flood emergencies — the highest level of flood warning — were issued Thursday morning for McCaysville, Georgia, in Fannin County, and Copperhill, Tennessee, in Polk County, on the Georgia-Tennessee border. Record flooding struck there along a river known as the Toccoa River in Georgia and the Ocoee River in Tennessee once it flows across the border. The river crested just above the previous record flood set in 1990 just after 6:00 a.m. ET in McCaysville and Copperhill, above the level that causes a “catastrophic flood event” in the two towns, according to the National Weather Service. The river has fallen several feet since then, but remained above flood stage as of late Thursday morning. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp said the state is leading a multi-agency response to the flooding, including “aviation and boat assets, as well as local counties and Tennessee first responders.” Emergency management in Fannin and Gilmer counties in Georgia have reported “multiple homes flooded and some completely surrounded by water” and water rescues. A state of emergency has been issued in McCaysville, and the city is closed until further notice, according to the city’s police chief Michael Earley. “We’re actively trying to water rescue people, and we’ve still got several people trapped in homes that we’re trying to get to,” Earley told CNN affiliate Atlanta News First. Evacuations were ordered for residents in McCaysville on West Tennessee Avenue and East Tennessee Avenue, where a Georgia DOT camera showed streets and buildings swamped by the flooded river. There were still “numerous residents” that needed evacuations in Fannin County, the county’s emergency management said early Thursday morning. Crews have been conducting rescues “all night long” the county Fire Chief Larry Thomas told CNN. At least two cars were swept away by floodwater, but their occupants were rescued uninjured, he said. On Thursday morning, crews were conducting a rescue at a home that had standing water up to the countertops, he added. Multiple roads are blocked by mudslides or have been washed away completely, and propane tanks have become dislodged and are floating in floodwater, according to Thomas. At least one propane tank was on fire in McCaysville, CNN affiliate WSB-TV reported. There were also at least four structure fires overnight, which Thomas believes were caused by lightning. Two of the structures, one a home, were lost after floodwater prevented fire trucks from responding. A separate flash flood emergency was also issued overnight for other parts of Fannin County and neighboring Gilmer County in Georgia. Water has also entered homes in Gilmer County, with knee-deep water covering roads in impacted residential areas, Aaron Freeman, the county emergency management director, told CNN Thursday morning. Crews rescued three people stranded in two houses, he said, and flooding has also cut off access to a small group of homes, but residents there have not reported any issues. Widespread rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches from slow-moving overnight storms were reported across parts of North Georgia, with over 8 inches in isolated spots. Up to 6 inches of rain fell in just six hours at multiple rain gauges in the area. This equates to at least a 1-in-200-year rainfall — a rate that has only a 0.5% chance of happening in a given year, under normal circumstances. Such extreme rainfall is becoming more common as planet-warming pollution pushes temperatures higher as warmer air can hold more moisture. The rain has come to an end across northern Georgia and southern Tennessee. No additional downpours are expected through the weekend, but dangerous river flooding will remain a threat throughout the day. East Coast next up for flood threat The wet weather will shift east and hit coastal portions of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic Thursday night into Saturday morning, with the heaviest rain expected on Friday. Widespread and significant flooding is unlikely because the ground is primed to soak up most of the rain after weeks of dryness. But some flooding could unfold if enough rain falls too fast. A Level 2 of 4 risk of flooding rain is in place for southern New England, where the brunt of the heaviest rain is forecast. Totals of 1 to 3 inches are expected there, but a few locations caught under repeated heavy downpours could deal with closer to 5 inches. It’s difficult to pinpoint exactly where that could occur until the storms are underway. Boston is just outside of this zone in a broader Level 1 of 4 flood threat in New England. Flooding is most likely in urban and low-lying areas that are less capable of handling heavy rain. In the Mid-Atlantic, a Level 1 of 4 risk of flooding rainfall is in place Friday in southeastern Virginia and northeastern North Carolina. There’s currently no outlooked flood threat along the Interstate 95 corridor from New York City to Washington, DC, but rain is likely there — especially very late Thursday night through Friday morning. Ponding on roadways and delays at area airports are possible. Most of the East Coast will dry out by Saturday afternoon, but some showers could develop deeper inland.

articles.title: Drones carrying drones: Turkey turns Bayraktar TB2 into flying weapons carrier
articles.summary: Turkey is giving its Bayraktar TB2 combat drone a new role, turning it into an airborne carrier for smaller kamikaze drones.
articles.body: Turkey is giving its Bayraktar TB2 combat drone a new role, turning it into an airborne carrier for smaller kamikaze drones. In a recent test, the Turkish unmanned aircraft carried 16 attack drones and released two of them to strike designated targets, demonstrating how a single drone could deploy multiple smaller weapons in the battlefield.According to Turkish defence company Baykar, the test was conducted at the Keşan Flight Training and Test Center in northwestern Türkiye. The Bayraktar TB2 carried 16 Skydagger first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drones during the flight, releasing two of them over a designated test area.Both drones struck their assigned targets, while the TB2 acted as an airborne communications relay, allowing ground-based operators to control the smaller attack drones independently.Haluk Bayraktar, CEO of Baykar, described the development as a potential shift in battlefield operations, saying the integration could significantly extend the reach of smaller attack drones."The Bayraktar TB2, carrying 16 Skydagger FPV drones and providing an airborne communications relay, is opening the door to a new doctrine on the battlefield," he said.He added that FPV drones, which typically have an average battlefield range of around 15 km, could reach targets thousands of kilometres away with the TB2 integration.The Bayraktar TB2 is a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) unmanned combat aerial vehicle developed by Turkey's Baykar. Designed to carry out intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision-strike missions, the drone combines long flight endurance with the ability to carry guided weapons.Its relatively low operating cost and combat record have made it one of Turkey's most widely exported military drones.It can carry a payload of up to 150 kg, including surveillance equipment and precision-guided munitions. Powered by a 100-horsepower engine, it has a maximum speed of 110 knots (204 kmph), a cruising speed of 90 knots (167 kmph) and an operational altitude of up to 16,000 feet.The aircraft has an endurance of more than 20 hours and a maximum operational range of 3,400 km. It supports both line-of-sight and beyond-line-of-sight communication systems, allowing it to operate over long distances.Why is this significant in modern warfare?The development reflects a changing approach to drone warfare, where larger unmanned aircraft are increasingly being used to deploy smaller, expendable attack drones.By turning the Bayraktar TB2 into an airborne carrier, Turkey could give relatively small FPV kamikaze drones greater reach without requiring them to cover the entire distance from a ground launch point. The TB2's ability to act as a communications relay could also help operators control these drones over distances that would otherwise be difficult to cover.The concept could also enable a single aircraft to carry multiple smaller attackers for separate strikes, offering greater flexibility in modern battlefield operations.

articles.title: Ancient discovery from time of Jesus emerges near Jerusalem's Temple Mount
articles.summary: A 2,000-year-old ritual bathing complex near Jerusalem's Temple Mount features three large mikva'ot where Jewish pilgrims purified before entering.
articles.body: Archaeologists have uncovered a remarkably well-preserved 2,000-year-old ritual bathing complex near Jerusalem's Temple Mount that dates back to the time of Jesus. It was likely used by Jewish pilgrims visiting the ancient holy site, with an expert noting the discovery helps highlight the broader significance of baptism. The excavation, announced earlier this fall, was carried out by archaeologists from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The discovery was made in the Ophel, an archaeological area immediately south of Jerusalem's Temple Mount, near an ancient entrance known as the Triple Gate. JESUS' CRUCIFIXION ACCOUNT GETS FRESH LOOK AFTER ANCIENT RING TIED TO PILATE IS REINTERPRETED The complex was built in the early first century A.D. It features three large ritual baths, a plastered pool and a paved plaza, along with an extensive water system. Located near the Triple Gate, one of the main entrances to the Temple Mount, the complex likely served pilgrims who underwent ritual purification before visiting the Second Temple, researchers said. Officials described one of the baths as "exceptionally well-preserved," noting that it stands nearly 14 feet tall and retains its original vaulted stone ceiling and a shaft that once supplied it with water. "The preservation of a Second Temple-period structure from floor to ceiling is exceedingly rare in Jerusalem, particularly in such a central and historically significant location," the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in a statement. HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS Excavation directors professor Uzi Leibner and professor Orit Peleg-Barkat described the monumental stone structure devoted entirely to ritual purification as "a truly unparalleled phenomenon." The archaeologists added, "The complex goes to the heart of our research into the archaeology of Second Temple-period pilgrimage: how the area immediately south of the Temple Mount was designed to accommodate the many pilgrims who came to Jerusalem to visit the Temple, and what activities and rituals took place near its gates." The complex also bears evidence of Jerusalem's destruction by Roman forces in 70 A.D. Archaeologists found dozens of coins dating to the First Jewish Revolt against Rome on the complex's floors and among the debris. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT Excavations also revealed an even older public purification facility beneath the complex, including another large ritual bath believed to date to the first century B.C. The earlier structure suggests the site had been used for ritual purification long before the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. "Baptism, a ritual that many people think of as exclusively Christian, emerged out of broader ancient Jewish bathing and purification rituals." While Jesus and his disciples could theoretically have visited the bathing complex, there is no evidence in the New Testament that they did, said Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Moss, who specializes in early Christianity, told Fox News Digital the discovery offers insight into the ancient Jewish purification practices that helped shape Christian baptism. Between the first century B.C. and the first century A.D., ritual bathing became increasingly popular among Jews in Judea and Galilee, as evidenced by the growing number of immersion facilities built during that period, Moss said. She pointed to the Qumran community, associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls, whose residents used ritual baths known as mikva'ot for daily bathing. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Moss said the broader interest in ritual bathing also helps explain the popularity of John the Baptist and the adoption of baptism by Jesus' followers. "What it does show is that baptism, a ritual that many people think of as exclusively Christian, emerged out of broader ancient Jewish bathing and purification rituals," Moss said. "That, in turn, can help explain the popularity of John the Baptist and the use of baptism by Jesus' followers." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The discovery comes amid a series of recent archaeological finds in Israel dating to the time of Jesus. Earlier this fall, Israeli officials announced the recovery of a remarkably intact 2,000-year-old Jewish ritual bath in Kiryat Gat, about 35 miles southwest of Jerusalem. articles.title: Top Republican condemns sentencing of ‘hero’ Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
articles.summary: Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Select Committee on China, condemned China’s sentencing of activist Joshua Wong, calling him a “hero.” A Hong Kong court sentenced Wong to 10 more years in prison under a Beijing-imposed national security law. “Joshua Wong is a hero who has stood up to an authoritarian superpower.…
articles.body:
Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Select Committee on China, condemned China’s sentencing of activist Joshua Wong, calling him a “hero.”

A Hong Kong court sentenced Wong to 10 more years in prison under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

“Joshua Wong is a hero who has stood up to an authoritarian superpower. Joshua only pleaded guilty to the baseless charge of foreign collusion because of the CCP’s systematic erosion of Hong Kong’s judicial independence. In return, the CCP has effectively sentenced him under its repressive National Security Law,” Moolenaar wrote in a statement , using an abbreviation for the Chinese Communist Party.

The Michigan Republican blasted the sentencing as “a shameless display of the CCP’s complete disregard for the universal human rights of life and liberty endowed to all of us by our Creator.”

He added that the international community’s support is needed “now more than ever” and demanded Wong be released “and reunited with his family.”

Moolenaar sponsored the activist for the Defending Freedoms Project at the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission in Congress, which shows support for international prisoners “unjustly imprisoned for their identity, beliefs, or peaceful expression,” according to the lawmaker .

Wong, 30, led student protests as a teenager as part of international efforts for the democracy movement in Hong Kong. He was expected to be released in January after already serving a more than four year prison sentence in connection with a prior massive national security case in the city.

He received more charges, including conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, in 2025.

The U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that Wong has been “unjustly imprisoned” since late 2020 and accused Beijing of going to “extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong.”

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing that Wong had pleaded guilty and that “relevant parties” should stop making remarks about the city’s judicial proceedings and not interfere.

The Hong Kong activist was the subject of the 2017 Netflix documentary “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower,” which focused on his founding of the Scholarism movement against pro-Chinese propaganda and his role in the Umbrella Movement protests in 2014, along with the launch of the pro-democracy political party Demosisto, The Independent reported.

After a pro-Beijing newspaper accused the documentary for “beautifying” his crimes, it reached the top of Netflix’s most-watched list in Hong Kong.

articles.title: A Florida man sold his Georgia home and paid money from a joint account toward a new marital house; after a two-year marriage ended, an appeals court ruled he could not get separate credit for that down payment
articles.summary: A home bought with money earned before marriage may seem to be a clear case of separate ownership.
articles.body: A home bought with money earned before marriage may seem to be a clear case of separate ownership. However, the legal character of those funds can change when they pass through a joint bank account and are then used to purchase property in both spouses' names. The distinction became central in a Florida divorce case where a man wanted to be repaid for money he had brought into the marriage. On Nov. 4, 2026, a Florida appeals court ruled that he could not claim separate credit for the down payment, though it upheld his right to recover certain housing expenses he paid after the couple separated.From Georgia Estate to House of MatrimonyThe Florida District Courts of Appeal said the dispute was between Melyza C. Anderson and Leland A. Anderson, who were divorced after a two-year marriage. Before they were in a relationship, Leland had a home in Georgia. Following their marriage, the couple decided to move to Florida and build a home in Tampa.To finance the move and construction, Leland sold his Georgia property and deposited the proceeds into a joint bank account held by the couple. He also transferred a lump sum of money earned through employment into the same account. Later, the couple took money from this joint account for the down payment on their new house.The property was registered in both spouses' names. But soon after the house was completed, Melyza filed for divorce and the question became how to treat the funds used to purchase the house in dividing the marital assets.Why the down payment became a bone of contentionIn the divorce proceedings, Leland sought financial credit for the money he originally contributed from his separate assets, the Florida District Courts of Appeal noted. He declared that the down payment should be considered nonmarital propertyMelyza challenged this, arguing that once the money was deposited into their joint account, mixed with other funds and used toward jointly owned property, it effectively became marital money.The trial court initially ruled in Leland’s favor, awarding him credit for the down payment and housing expenses he paid after the separation. Melyza then appealed the decision.In reviewing the financial dispute, the appeals court looked at Florida's rules on classifying marital and nonmarital assets. It noted that money deposited in a joint account can lose its separate identity through commingling. Depositing individually owned funds into a shared account also creates a rebuttable presumption that the other spouse receives a one-half interest in the money.Court distinguishes two claimsThe appeals court held that Leland had not shown by clear and convincing evidence that he intended to keep the funds as separate property. Instead, the money had gone into a joint account and was used to buy a house titled in both spouses' names.Thus, the down payment was classified as marital property and the trial court erred in giving him separate credit.But the court reached a different conclusion about the expenses Leland paid post-separation. Though he moved out, he continued paying the mortgage and other expenses related to the property for about two years before trial. Melyza stayed in the house but did not help maintain it.The trial court found Melyza had enough income to contribute and did not need temporary support, and the Florida District Courts of Appeal upheld the reimbursement.Appeal court upheld divorce but reversed the down payment. The matter was remanded to the trial judge for a recalculation of the couple's equitable distribution.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Her Princess Diana collection is built on manifestation. And a few re-mortgages
articles.summary: Renae Plant is thought to have one of the world’s largest private collections of the late royal’s belongings.
articles.body: Renae Plant and her husband Livinio Stuyck were about to become restaurant investors. A local pizza place in their Los Angeles neighborhood had approached the couple, offering them the opportunity to own a small stake. It made sense: Plant and Stuyck had a nest egg already saved and some comparable experience in business; Plant has been the director and owner of the local Camelot Kids Preschool since 2008. “And then my best friend Kevin says, ‘Hey Renae, six of Diana’s dresses are at Julien’s,’” an auction house. “’You want to come have a look?’” she says with a wry eyebrow raise over video call. Twelve years and more than 800 dresses, accessories and objects later, Plant believes she has cultivated one of the largest private collections of Princess Diana’s personal belongings in the world. “That was a miracle,” she said. “Because any day later and that would have gone in a different direction.” This sense of divine intervention has followed Plant throughout her life. Her first brush with the late Princess of Wales was in 1983 while on a school trip to a ginger factory in Queensland, Australia. “I was beside myself, because I’d fallen in love with her when she got married, and the fairy tale,” she said. “Every girl’s dream was to marry a prince, back in the day.” But Plant, then just one of many 12-year-old schoolgirls waiting in line to meet Diana during her royal visit, got more than the standard handshake. After slipping away from her classmates and following Diana under a barricade, she realized the princess had dropped something: a small, palm-sized clay platypus. A kindly policeman told her it was fated. Since then, Plant has needed no further encouragement, dedicating much of her life to Princess Diana’s memory. “I look back on that platypus moment and it was almost like it was meant to be,” she said. In 2018, she set up The Princess & The Platypus Foundation; a registered non-profit that supports charities aligned with the kind of philanthropic work Diana carried out while alive. “It’s my job to protect her life and legacy, and to share it with the world,” Plant said. Part of that mission is consolidating as many of the princess’ possessions as possible. “I felt like all of Diana’s pieces were just being scattered aimlessly all around the world,” she said. Plant in the past has bid against, and beat, the Historic Royal Palaces charity in London, who alongside managing unoccupied royal palaces in the UK also conserve and display royal ceremonial dress. She has also lent them dresses. Plant believes luck, manifestation or something larger, has helped build her impressive vault. Take last year, when she bought the “caring dress” –– the vivid floral Belville Sassoon frock Diana often wore to brighten up visits to children’s hospitals –– for $520,000 at auction. Plant was surprised that the signature dress, something she saw Diana wear in person in 1988, didn’t sell for more money. “The universe was out there,” she said. Her assigned bidder’s number was 333, “an Angel number. She was definitely looking down over me. And some internet thing happened.” She recalls a network issue meaning the underbidder couldn’t match her at the crucial moment. When she realized she’d won, Plant made the news when she was filmed collapsing with joy. “It’s a nerve-wracking situation,” she said. “I get shaky.” The rest of her success as a Lady Di collector can be attributed to more tangible personal sacrifices. “My husband is a very loving man, because he lets us take the mortgage out against our home every now and again,” she said. They re-mortgaged in 2015, when Plant had her heart set on Diana’s studded Atelier Versace gown which she bought at auction for $200,000, and again in 2025. That extra line of equity last summer meant Plant could pick up the Belleville Sassoon dress, and another 34 items including a peach-colored ostrich feather hat Diana wore on her honeymoon which Plant bought for $26,000. The couple spent around $1.9 million that day. (In general, Plant prefers not to focus on the monetary value of her pieces and refused to give a total estimate of the collection.) But while her husband Stuyck is a benevolent financier, Plant maintains he is a terrible underbidder. She’s still sore about the 1981 Warm & Wonderful black sheep sweater she lost out on due to letting Stuyck press the buttons. It sold for a record-breaking $1.14 million. “I should never let my husband bid,” she said, and laughed. Thankfully, Diana had two of the sheep knits made — and Plant got her hands on the second one. When we talk, she is preparing for her very first exhibition, “The Princess Diana: Love, Life and Legacy — A Life of Giving,” opening at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum on Saturday. To fill the three-act showcase, tracing Diana’s life from childhood up to her untimely death in 1997, Plant has emptied out her entire collection. There will be personal letters, Diana’s baby dresses, the tape recorders she made voice memos on, her favorite childhood records (ABBA, Queen and Elton John, if you’re curious) and of course, her many, many gowns. Almost everything on show, from Diana’s enormous taffeta “spare” wedding dress to the embellished black Jacques Azagury evening gown she wore to her 36th birthday party, belongs to Plant. The exception is a certain velvet gown Diana wore while being twirled on the dance floor by John Travolta during President Reagan’s White House dinner in 1985. That is rented. “It’s the only piece we’re loaning,” she said. “It’s going to steal the thunder!” Diana’s off-the-shoulder mermaid tale gown will be displayed alongside Nancy Reagan’s ivory James Galanos dress. Her day job as a director of a local preschool means the agony and ecstasy of six figure bidding wars happens largely after Plant has clocked off. “I put in a whole day at my preschool, and then I come home at night and do it on the weekends,” she said. The couple also pay out of pocket for a monthly subscription to store and preserve the pieces in climate-controlled facilities, which charge per item. Plant currently catalogues her collection in an online museum accessible to paid members. The high financial stakes might put others off, but something elusive keeps Plant going. “What I’m doing is higher than me. I’m a vessel. I’m channeling,” she said. “It’s an energetic thing for me. I don’t even know how I could do it. I don’t even know how things have ended up this way, but they have.” On December 5, exactly 12 years to the day Plant bought her first dress worn by Diana, another gown is set to go on auction. The “revenge dress,” that show-stopping Christina Stambolian gown that launched a thousand superlatives: the princess’ sexiest, most famous, most rebellious outfit. Sotheby’s New York has set a price estimate of $300,000. “I can’t afford that,” Plant said. “I’ve already tapped my mortgage out for a while. It’s sad. My thing is to really put all these pieces back together, so it does break my heart when I’m not able to.” Instead, the Reagan Library will be the first to publicly unveil another dress from Plant’s collection with a similar post-divorce vim. It has many of the same design features of Stambolian’s frock, a sensual sweetheart neckline in a color previously off-limits to royals: black. (Official dress codes mandate that black is restricted to periods of mourning — when Diana was no longer part of the royal family, LBD’s were back on the menu.) Designed by Azagury, this dress was perhaps the last Diana ever commissioned. The late princess had six fittings in total for the gown, including one just days before her death in August 1997. She never got to wear the finished product. “The pins are still in the back of that dress,” said Plant. “It’s a beautiful finale, so to speak.”

articles.title: Burning rubbish chokes besieged Yemeni city of Taiz
articles.summary: Taiz residents face health risks as waste accumulates amid sniper fire, forcing people to burn it in the streets.
articles.body:
Taiz, Yemen — Black smoke from burning rubbish envelops the Usaifira area north of the Yemeni city of Taiz, while foul odours fill the air in surrounding residential neighbourhoods.

Along a waterway known as the al-Saeed stream, bags of uncollected household waste pile up – a scene that has become part of daily life for residents. They find themselves trapped between mounds of rubbish and smoke, in a crisis that not only reflects a breakdown in public services but poses a direct threat to their health and environmental safety.

Since early October, the city has seen a buildup of waste, with sanitation trucks unable to reach the main landfill site in the western part of the city controlled by Iranian-backed Houthi forces, who have laid siege to the city for a month, affecting hundreds of thousands of people. Fighting has escalated since October 5, when forces of the internationally recognised government — backed by a Saudi-led military coalition — launched a major military offensive aimed at taking back all areas of the country under Houthi control.

Sanitation workers in Taiz say that snipers have been deployed in the vicinity of the landfill, and that staff have faced gunfire more than once while trying to reach the site to empty their trucks, preventing waste disposal operations.

The disruption comes as the city suffers from an acute shortage of fuel, which has further hampered waste collection. As a result, rubbish has accumulated on streets and in storm drains, prompting desperate residents to set the waste on fire.

The tide of rubbish extends into the stream from the middle of lower Tahrir Street down to the Usaifira area, in the middle of neighbourhoods where residents are exposed to toxic fumes every day.

Rather than a collection point, the al-Saeed stream has become a smoke-filled dumping ground, with fires igniting periodically and fumes drifting towards adjacent homes.

“This causes us suffocation and diseases, young and old. The children suffocate from the smoke,” Usaifira resident Abdo Hadi told Al Jazeera. “It is a foul smell, and on top of that they burn it.”

Hadi said the buildup and burning of waste are threatening the lives of his family and other residents, making already difficult living conditions even worse.

“We are besieged from every side, [with] neither gas nor petrol, and a black market,” he said.

Taiz generates between 550 and 600 tonnes of waste daily, or about 16,500 to 18,000 tonnes per month. Mohammed Ibrahim, director of a cleaning initiative in Taiz, told Al Jazeera that waste collection has been severely affected since October 5.

Ibrahim said the cleaning initiative has also suffered from funding cuts, while supplies needed to carry out its work have been disrupted.

A sanitation worker described the grim reality while emptying a truck in Usaifira: “We are here with the rubbish in the Usaifira stream because of the war, and the people here are exposed to diseases from the rubbish, and we pile the waste in the stream, leave it to God.”

The waste crisis is part of a wider breakdown of basic services in the city. On October 20, Laurent Bukera, the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen, expressed deep concern over the “rapidly deteriorating humanitarian and economic situation in Taiz”.

Bukera warned that road closures and insecurity were preventing vital supplies, including fuel, from entering the city and surrounding areas, leaving the health system “close to collapse”.

Emphasising the severe impact on hundreds of thousands of families, he warned that water production in the city has halved and alternatives are running out. Bukera called directly on the Houthis to urgently open safe passage for commercial goods, food, medicine, and humanitarian assistance in areas that they control.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has warned of an escalating humanitarian crisis in Taiz, saying conflict has cut off lifesaving assistance to 800,000 people, including 600,000 who depend on aid in the city.

El-Khidir Daloum, WFP representative and country director in Yemen, underlined the severity of the blockade.

“We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it,” Daloum said. “This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most.”

The blockade has also decimated local resources.

“Access roads have been cut off and that means that very little fuel, food or other supplies have reached the city since,” said Jens Laerke, spokesman for the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

He explained that water production has fallen dramatically and the cost of trucked water has tripled.

“So, you can imagine what that does to these people who are trapped there,” Laerke added.

Health risks are multiplying rapidly in this polluted environment.

UNICEF has raised concerns about widespread hunger, saying it screened more than 168,000 children in Taiz this year, with more than 52,000 found to be acutely malnourished. Ricardo Pires, a spokesman for the UN children’s agency, warned of logistical hurdles.

“Even when stocks are available, access constraints and disruptions to supply routes can make it more difficult for partners to transport supplies and for families to safely reach treatment,” Pires said.

articles.title: Garlic bread, stolen trucks and a handwritten apology: Inside a convicted killer’s 10 days on the run
articles.summary: Authorities on Wednesday were still trying to piece together how an escaped Tennessee prisoner convicted of murder evaded capture for more than a week before being tracked down hundreds of miles away in Missouri.
articles.body: Authorities on Wednesday were still trying to piece together how an escaped Tennessee prisoner convicted of murder evaded capture for more than a week before being tracked down hundreds of miles away in Missouri. Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was apprehended Tuesday near Kansas City, Missouri, authorities said. Morley was found after troopers used roadside cameras and a helicopter to track him down and his truck got stuck in the mud. Two rifles and a shotgun were recovered from the truck. Authorities believe Morley found his way to a farm near Marion, Illinois — about 127 miles (204 kilometers) away — in the days after his escape, spending some time in a shed that was used periodically by hunters. Investigators found evidence that he drank beer and prepared garlic bread and other food — and that he left behind an apologetic handwritten note after stealing a truck from the farm, according to Williamson County Sheriff Jeff Diederich. Morley is also suspected of stealing clothes and the three firearms from the property. Diederich believes Morley walked about 3 miles (5 kilometers) to the farm after abandoning a different truck he had driven after his escape. Security cameras captured Morley walking away from the truck and at a couple of locations along Route 13, but the terrain — which includes fields and woods — would have made it tough for him to be spotted, Diederich said. It’s unclear why Morley traveled to Marion and why he was driving near Kansas City, more than 350 miles (563 kilometers) away. “How he ended up in Marion is kind of a mystery,” Diederich said. Diederich said there's no evidence Morley had help from anyone. Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee’s far northwestern corner on Oct. 25, after he slipped through a fence in his prison clothes. Surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned in Marion. Kim Wheeler-Elder, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, wrote in a text message that all “available information” regarding Morley’s whereabouts when he was on the run has been released. The Missouri State Highway Patrol says it was informed Tuesday morning that Morley was possibly traveling west on Interstate 70 in the Kansas City area. Authorities said he was compliant when he was arrested. Morley was transported to the Lafayette County jail in Lexington, Missouri, according to Justin Ewing, a spokesperson for the Missouri State Highway Patrol. The Lafayette County Sheriff's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. No charges have been filed against him in Missouri courts, according to online court records. Before Morley was apprehended, he was charged in federal court in Tennessee with one count of unlawful flight to avoid prosecution, court documents show. Morley was also charged Tuesday in federal court in Missouri with one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. A deputy U.S. marshal interviewed Morley at the Lafayette County jail on Tuesday and Morley admitted to escaping the Tennessee prison, stealing the truck in Marion as well as the two rifles and shotgun, according to a probable cause affidavit. District Attorney General Danny Goodman Jr. in Tennessee said in a phone interview that he plans to file additional charges but it's unclear when Morley will be returned to Tennessee. Morley was convicted of killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. ___ Kelety reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, contributed.

articles.title: Actor and comedian Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: British actor, comedian and media personality Russell Brand faces a lengthy prison sentence after he was found guilty in a London court on Thursday of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women.
articles.body: British actor, comedian and media personality Russell Brand faces a lengthy prison sentence after he was found guilty in a London court on Thursday of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women. Brand, 51, was convicted of raping the 21-year-old admirer in 2009 after they met at one of his shows in west London. He was also found guilty of groping an MTV worker at a bar in central London in 2004, kissing and groping another woman at her workplace in 2005 and sexually assaulting another woman in 2009 when she was forced to give him a massage. At Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, a jury of eight men and four women cleared the star of two separate charges of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault, after deliberating for around eight and a half hours. Speaking after the verdicts were delivered, judge Joel Bennathan said the case was “very well prepared,” according to Britain’s Press Association (PA), adding that sentencing would take place on Monday. Brand, who stood straight in the dock as the verdicts were revealed and closed his eyes as he heard he was found guilty of rape, has been remanded in custody. “The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term,” Bennathan said. Brand said “I love you” to his wife Laura Gallacher, an author and illustrator who consistently attended court with her husband, before he entered the dock to hear the verdicts. Brand, who was previously married to US pop star Katy Perry, “used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” London’s Metropolitan Police Service said following the comedian’s conviction. “As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be,” Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said in a statement. The Met also confirmed investigations are continuing regarding two other allegations of rape made against Brand, according to PA. Speaking outside court, David Roberts of the Crown Prosecution Service said the evidence showed Brand “to be a calculated sexual predator, using his growing fame and power to create situations in which he could pursue women sexually regardless of what they wanted.” Accusers say Brand transformed during alleged attacks His accusers appeared in court over the past three weeks, revealing in emotional testimony how Brand forced them into sexual activity at a time when he was rising to fame as one of Britain’s best-known stand-up comedians and TV presenters. Detectives had started looking into the comedian in 2023 after allegations were made in a joint investigation by three British media outlets – The Sunday Times, The Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches” program. Brand also denied those allegations, which related to multiple women who were not involved in the criminal trial. A number of women who were not known to each other came forward to officers with reports concerning Brand after that investigation was published, the Met Police said. During the trial, prosecutors argued that Brand was a “sexual predator” who was pursing a mission to have sex with 5,000 women. Brand recognized that he had been obsessed with sex then but said that consent in sex was “fundamental.” The trial against Brand opened in London in mid-October. One of the complainants told the court how the pair had met after a gig at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009. She said the pair had engaged in a consensual threesome at the venue before she went to his townhouse for sex several days later. However, she said their second meeting turned into rape when he forced her into anal sex and ignored her pleas to stop. The woman said she had turned to alcoholism in the wake of the incident. One of her friends described her as a “bright, bubbly and confident girl” but said “this experience definitely changed her,” according to PA. Another woman told the court she “felt ashamed” and that the comedian acted “like nothing happened” after he groped her at a party at a bar in Soho, central London, in 2004. Riding a wave of controversy to Hollywood Brand started his career in showbiz as a stand-up comedian, drawing on his own experiences with illegal drugs and sex addiction for his performances. He became a British household name in the early 2000s as the host of “Celebrity Big Brother’s Big Mouth,” a spin-off of “Celebrity Big Brother.” Brand’s chaotic energy, unfiltered language and provocative jokes made him a divisive pop culture personality, with the public split on loving or hating his act. In 2001, he was fired from MTV UK after turning up to work dressed as Osama bin Laden two days after the September 11 terror attacks. He later attributed his behavior to his addiction to crack cocaine and heroin. Brand went to rehab in 2002 and says he has remained sober since. In 2006, he moved to mainstream radio with “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 2, a weekly Saturday night program during which he had frank, comedic – and often X-rated – conversations with a co-host and guests. However, the popular radio show ended abruptly two years later with Brand’s exit following the broadcast of sexist and misogynistic voice messages to “Fawlty Towers” star Andrew Sachs, which sparked outrage and breached UK broadcasting regulations. But the scandal didn’t halt Brand’s rise to global stardom. He went on to star in several Hollywood movies including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.” He was married to Perry, the US pop star, between 2010 and 2012. In the past decade, Brand has shifted away from his eccentric, sex-forward image and started making podcasts around spirituality, meditation and yoga. In 2017, he wrote a self-help guide, “Recovery: Freedom From Our Addictions,” while his performances moved from theater stages to wellness gatherings. That same year, he married Gallacher, with whom he has three children. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, he has cultivated something of a cult following online, with more than 6.6 million subscribers to his YouTube channel and a show on the new platform Rumble. He was living in Florida and became a born-again Christian, in 2026 publishing a book on his conversion through conservative commentator Tucker Carlson’s new imprint.

articles.title: The Russell Brand I saw in court was not the flamboyant character most people will know
articles.summary: Brand stood upright in the dock as the verdicts were read out in court - ending this sometimes surreal trial.
articles.body:
This was not the Russell Brand most people will remember from the height of his noughties TV and comedy fame.

The flamboyant character with big gestures and provocative one-liners was not the man we saw in the courtroom.

During his rape trial, Brand mostly sat impassively in the dock, staring straight ahead. His stillness was striking. His face betrayed no visible emotion or reaction as the string of allegations against him were outlined in detail over several days.

After a three-week trial, the 51-year-old was found guilty of one charge of rape and three charges of sexual assault. He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations spanned a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involved six female complainants.

More women likely to come forward, says detective who led Russell Brand investigation

Russell Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

The Brand on show in this trial seemed courteous to a fault.

Yet the polite, respectful man we saw holding doors open and thanking court staff was in striking contrast to the evidence we heard.

His victims told of a brash, arrogant, sexually voracious man who did not take no for an answer from the women he preyed on; a ruthless rapist and manipulative sex offender.

Flashes of the Brand we were used to seeing in the media were not totally absent - they often manifested themselves in the morning when he would arrive at Southwark Crown Court.

Mostly dressed in variations of dark jackets and trousers, long scarves and open-neck shirts, he would often make a beeline for the media scrum outside the courthouse.

On day one of the trial, he confidently uttered the words: "Today, I feel blessed. I feel of course concerned, but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved. That's my prayer."

In all my years of covering court cases I've never seen a defendant address journalists during a trial. His professed hatred for the mainstream media clearly did not stop him from having his say.

Sitting on the floor of a court corridor in the early days of the trial, I was tapping on my phone when Brand walked past.

"Hello, mate!" came his cheery greeting. It was a bizarre moment given the seriousness of his situation. I continued typing.

In another slightly surreal moment a black people carrier pulled up outside the court on the day the trial began.

The door to the car slid open and out stepped a man who looked just like Brand - but it wasn't him.

The mystery man attracted a few shouted questions before Brand stepped out of the car behind him.

The man was present on most days of the trial and wandered around after Brand, attracting double-takes and much comment, with no clarity about who he actually was.

Brand now positions himself as a Christian influencer and has been public about his faith. It was on display during his trial via the crucifixes of varying sizes that he wore. One day, I saw him handling what looked like prayer beads.

The court room itself was typical. The judge faced Brand, who sat in a long glass box with a door at one end, which was mostly left open, giving him a view of his wife.

I was directly behind him - no more than a metre and a half away in the press seats. Between Brand and the judge, sat two sets of lawyers with the jury sitting immediately to the right of the judge.

Day after day we listened to harrowing and graphic accounts of rape and sexual abuse by Brand, some of the worst kinds imaginable.

The courage of the women who told their stories in court, who spoke behind a screen, was remarkable. The tears flowed, their nerves evident in their voices. The way they told their stories was deeply moving.

In the dock Brand's statue-like demeanour was broken only occasionally, when, during some of the evidence, he closed his eyes for several seconds, perhaps in silent prayer or meditation. There was no fidgeting or movement. He didn't flinch.

He maintained his composure even during some of the most harrowing evidence, when one of the victims told the court how blood and faeces had been left on Brand's bed sheets after he had raped her at his house.

During the testimony, Brand let out a sigh and looked at the ceiling with his eyes closed.

Speculation grew about whether Brand would give evidence - defendants can choose whether to take to the stand in their trials. It became a daily talking point among the reporters.

Giving evidence yourself can be a double-edged sword; a chance to vigorously defend one's innocence on the one hand, balanced by the risk of being torn apart by the prosecution barrister.

But it finally happened. Brand took to the witness box on day 10 of the trial. His testimony was perhaps unsurprising - after all, nobody apart from his wife had been prepared to speak up for him in court as part of the defence's case.

Brand entered the witness box wearing a dark suit and a white open-necked shirt. It was a nervous beginning. In an unusually loud voice he answered "no" to each of the allegations that were put to him.

He had taken his bible oath loudly too and stood, bolt upright with hands clasped behind his back.

I watched him like a hawk. This was a TV personality who was very much part of my youth, but now being interrogated with his liberty on the line.

His nerves seemed to visibly ease, so much so that at one point he put his hands in his pockets. It was noticeable that after an adjournment, he was back in his ramrod style stance with hands out of his pockets, behind his back.

The trial had hinged on the issue of consent. During his testimony Brand stated that "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

But many of his answers were terse, followed sometimes by silences. This led the prosecution to suggest it had been because he was finding the questions difficult to answer.

There were flashes of irritability. "Do you accept you were desperate for it [sex] and sometimes couldn't function without it?" he was asked. "No", he replied, displaying an apparent frustration at the repetitive nature of the questioning.

There were moments of bizarre levity too. When his wife, Laura, gave evidence in his defence, he laughed out loud from the dock when she spoke about them having plenty of friends and being grateful for them. It was the only moment throughout the trial where Brand had shown any visible emotion.

His wife attended court with him every day - soberly dressed, she sometimes took notes when the complainants were giving evidence.

Her support for her husband was visible - holding his hand as they walked in, smiling at him while he was in the dock for hours at a time.

Brand's minder often sat next to her in the public benches, and her father, former Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher sat with her in the gallery during the defence closing. Brand's father, Ron, also attended regularly, exchanging polite chat with some of the media.

At 51 years of age, Brand looked gaunt and visibly thinner as the trial neared its end, he seemed to have lost weight as the days went on. Other reporters said the same. We discussed whether signs of confidence he showed at the start had slowly ebbed away.

The verdicts came on Thursday after the jury had been deliberating for eight hours and 30 minutes.

Brand, who stood upright in the dock, showed limited emotion as the verdicts were read out. "Sit down Mr Brand," the judge told him after the verdicts were delivered.

"On what happens next," he added, "obviously a custodial sentence of some length will result."

Brand mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he was led away.

But his appearance in court was an extraordinary fall from grace. A man hailed as a multi-media celebrity, a self-confessed ladies' man too, but now a convicted rapist in custody.
